item.research_question: How do crystal structure, alloy composition, grain size, and twin boundary distance influence the mechanical characteristics, deformation mechanisms, and microstructure evolution of AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys during nanoimprinting?
item.material_system: AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys (specifically Al0.3, Al0.4, Al0.5, and Al0.7 compositions in FCC structure)
item.processing_route: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation using LAMMPS with EAM potential for interatomic interactions and Lennard-Jones potential for punch-sample interaction; punch moved at 25 m/s to 30 Å penetration depth at 300 K
item.test_conditions: Temperature: 300 K; Loading speed: 25 m/s; Penetration depth: 30 Å; Time step: 1.0 fs; Crystal structures: monocrystalline, polycrystalline, nano-twinned polycrystalline; Grain sizes: 51.43–80.03 Å; Twin boundary distances: 6.61–30.42 Å
key_findings: Highest imprinting forces were 830.20 nN (polycrystalline), 866.92 nN (NT-polycrystalline), and 930.38 nN (monocrystalline).
Maximum imprinting force increased with Al content: 736.20 nN (Al0.3), 778.04 nN (Al0.4), 830.20 nN (Al0.5), and 877.67 nN (Al0.7).
Reverse Hall–Petch relation observed for polycrystalline structure where smaller grain sizes (51.43 Å) resulted in lower loading forces (730.07 nN) compared to larger grains (80.03 Å, 879.45 nN).
Hall–Petch and reverse Hall–Petch relations found for NT-polycrystalline: peak force 866.92 nN at 13.16 Å TB distance, dropping to 679.90 nN at 6.61 Å.
Shear strain and local stress concentrated around the punch and on grain/twin boundaries (GBs/TBs).
Elastic recovery ratio was insensitive to alloy composition and grain size changes.
Formability of the pattern was higher with a decrease in twin boundary (TB) distance.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that grain boundaries (GBs) and twin boundaries (TBs) inhibit dislocation movement and plastic deformation. In polycrystalline structures, the slide and twist of GBs control deformation, while in NT-polycrystalline structures, TB migration and the interaction of dislocations with TBs are dominant. The presence of TBs enhances grain stability and strength up to a critical distance, after which excessive TBs lead to softening (reverse Hall–Petch).
item.limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study.
item.future_work: The text does not explicitly state future work proposed by the authors.
quotes: The reverse Hall–Petch relation found for the polycrystalline structure, while the Hall–Petch and reverse Hall–Petch relations are discovered in the NT-polycrystalline, which is due to the interactions between the dislocations and grain/twin boundaries (GBs/TBs).
The imprinting force increases as the Al content in the alloy increases.
The slide and twist of the GBs play a major in controlling the deformation mechanism of polycrystalline structure.
